source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence
finding: First large field audit of real intelligence forecasts. 1,514 unconditional forecasts from 15 analysts in a Canadian strategic intelligence unit, 2005-2011, scored against outcomes coded later by outside experts.
numbers: Source pool: 3,881 coded judgments, 2,315 unconditional forecasts, 1,943 with numeric probability, 1,562 with clear outcome (80.4%), 1,514 kept after dropping 30 team forecasts and 18 with missing data. 7 of 15 analysts were senior and wrote about 68%.
quote: The results show that both discrimination and calibration of forecasts was very good.
limits: One unit, one region (Middle East and Africa). Forecasts are organisational products reviewed by managers, not solo judgments.
agent_relevance: Real, reviewed, accountable reasoning can be well calibrated. A review stage plus numeric probabilities may be part of why. Scoring needs outcomes coded by someone outside the forecasting process.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) headline accuracy numbers
finding: Discrimination and Brier score were high. About 94% of forecasts fell on the correct side of 50%.
numbers: ROC area A = 0.940 (SE 0.007). Mean Brier 0.074. Brier decomposition: variance index 0.240, discrimination index 0.182. Normalised discrimination (eta squared) 0.758. Calibration index 0.016. Calibration-in-the-large 3.6e-5.
limits: Probability scale was coarse: 0, 1, 2.5, 4, 5, 6, 7.5, 9, 10 out of 10. Many questions were low-variance, so a low Brier is easier to reach.
agent_relevance: Our agent should report discrimination (AUC) and calibration separately, not one score. A coarse probability grid was enough for good results.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) underconfidence and recalibration
finding: Miscalibration was mostly underconfidence, not overconfidence. Harder and more important forecasts were more underconfident. A simple recalibration removed most of the error.
numbers: Mean signed calibration deviation (CCI) -0.076 (99% CI -0.082 to -0.070). Harder vs easier median -0.106 vs -0.044 (Z = -13.39). Greater vs lesser importance -0.071 vs -0.044. Karmarkar transform with fitted a = 2.2 cut the calibration index to 0.0018; mean absolute deviation fell from 12.7% to 4.2% (-66.9%). Feasible remap back to the 10-point scale: deviation 4.6% (-63.8%).
quote: Miscalibration was mainly due to underconfidence
limits: Recalibration was fitted and judged on the same forecasts. The authors warn about overfitting and about double correction if consumers already adjust.
agent_relevance: Post-hoc recalibration in code (G5) is a cheap, evidenced step. For LLM agents the sign can flip or hedge toward the middle (see a13, a17). Fit the correction per model on held-out data; never assume the direction.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) moderators: seniority, difficulty, importance
finding: Senior analysts discriminated better than junior ones. Easier forecasts were discriminated better than harder ones. Importance and time frame did not change discrimination.
numbers: Senior vs junior A = 0.951 (SE 0.008) vs 0.909 (SE 0.017), Z = 2.24, P = 0.025. Easier vs harder A = 0.966 (SE 0.010) vs 0.913 (SE 0.011), Z = 3.57, P < 0.001. Importance and time frame P > 0.25. Experience had no effect on underconfidence (P > 0.15).
limits: Seniority coded by one expert: 0-4 years junior, over 4 senior. Difficulty labelled after the fact by experts (criteria in the supplement). Tetlock and Mellers ask 'harder than what?'.
agent_relevance: Skill does track experience here, unlike in Tetlock's earlier expert study. Difficulty should be rated before the outcome is known, otherwise it is circular.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) sensitivity analyses and the Tetlock comparison
finding: Result survives pessimistic coding of ambiguous cases. The authors compare with Tetlock's 2005 expert study and claim higher resolution here.
numbers: Ambiguous outcomes (about 20% of numeric forecasts) coded 0.25/0.50/0.75 raised Brier to 0.090. Verbal-only forecasts (about 16%) set to 0.50 gave Brier 0.097. Best forecasters in Tetlock's study explained about 20% of outcome variance; here 76%. Calibration deviation about 25% smaller than in Tetlock.
limits: Cross-study comparison is crude: different question sets, horizons and base rates. Outcome coding by two outside experts with 90% agreement on 50 overlapping forecasts.
agent_relevance: Even under the worst coding the Brier stays below 0.10, but the comparison to Tetlock is not like for like. Keep abstentions and vague answers in the scoring, scored at 0.5.

source: Tetlock and Mellers (2014) Judging political judgment (PNAS reply)
finding: Reply to Mandel and Barnes by the Good Judgment Project leaders. They accept the data but dispute the reading: short horizons, low-variance questions, and post-hoc difficulty labels.
numbers: Mandel and Barnes horizons: 59% under 6 months, 96% under a year. Tetlock's poor results were mostly long-range (often 5 years plus). Over half of the Canadian questions scored Brier 0 or 0.01. 55% were labelled 'harder'. GJP best teams reached Brier scores 'similar to those of Canadian analysts' on similar horizons.
quote: Getting a good Brier score by predicting weather in a low-variance world
limits: No specific tournament Brier values are given. Cost claims (about $5M a year vs more than $5B for the IC) are rhetorical.
agent_relevance: Score comparisons across studies are only valid with matched horizon and base rate. We need a base-rate-aware metric (see a22, a26).

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence
finding: Argues that intelligence tradecraft (structured analytic techniques) was built without accuracy tests and may add noise. Recommends outside testing, recalibration, aggregation and accuracy tracking.
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Kent (1964): colleagues read 'serious possibility' as anywhere from 1:4 to 4:1 odds. Reports that coherence-based recalibration (Karvetski 2013) and coherentising then aggregating (Mandel et al. 2018) improved accuracy, and that analysts trained in ACH were more prone to unpacking effects.
limits: Review and position paper. Effect sizes are in the cited papers, which were not opened.
agent_relevance: Support for code-side correction (recalibrate, aggregate, check coherence) over adding judged steps. Matches G5 and the schema's 'not to add' list.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Good Judgment Project's three interventions: training, teaming, tracking. All improved calibration and resolution; statistical aggregation helped further. Only the abstract record was opened.
numbers: Five university teams in a 2-year IARPA tournament. Tracking put the top 2% of Year-1 performers into elite teams. No effect sizes in the abstract.
quote: Training, teaming, and tracking are psychological interventions that dramatically increased the accuracy of forecasts.
limits: Abstract only. Full effect sizes (Brier gaps by condition) were not read this session.
agent_relevance: Teaming and training are human-process effects. For one agent the analogue is scripted reference-class training and structured disagreement, but only with independent samples (G4).

source: Good Judgment Project overview (secondary)
finding: Secondary summary: IARPA ACE started July 2011, GJP won both seasons and was the only team funded from summer 2013. Claims of margin over other teams and over analysts with classified access.
numbers: '35% to 72% more accurate than any other research team'. Top forecasters 'reportedly 30% better' than officers with classified access. IARPA-ACE posed about 100 to 150 questions a year.
limits: Wikipedia, not a primary source. The 30% claim rests on press reports and is unverified here. No Brier values given.
agent_relevance: Treat the 'beat the CIA' number as unverified. Cite only primary tournament scores for performance.

source: Satopaa and Ungar (2015) Combining and extremizing real-valued forecasts
finding: Shows that a non-trivial weighted average of forecasts is never optimal and must be pushed away from the marginal mean (extremized). Gives a linear extremizing method. Authors are from the IARPA-funded GJP team.
numbers: Theory plus synthetic and real data examples; extremizing improved aggregation in each. Rain example: if rain falls on 20% of days and the average forecast is 0.30, moving the aggregate toward 0 or 1 improves it only under conditions on the marginal mean. Cites beta-transform (Ranjan and Gneiting 2010) and logit model (Satopaa 2014) for probabilities.
limits: Extremizing helps when forecasters hold partly different information. If they share the same information, or errors are correlated, it is not justified by this theory.
agent_relevance: Our schema G4 forbids extremizing LLM votes. This paper gives the reason: extremizing assumes each forecaster adds independent information; samples from one model do not.

source: Satopaa and Ungar (2015) information structure example
finding: Worked example where forecasters jointly know 80% of the total information but the revealed aggregator captures far less.
numbers: In the paper's example the group knows 80% of the total information; the revealed aggregator knows only 32% of it (as read from the text near lines 493-504 of the converted PDF).
limits: Stylised model, not tournament data. Setup text read; full derivation not checked.
agent_relevance: Shows why plain averaging under-uses information when sources differ. With overlapping LLM samples there is little distinct information to recover.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Retrieval plus reasoning plus trimmed-mean ensemble system, fine-tuned on forecasts that beat the crowd. Test set has only questions after the models' knowledge cutoffs (June 2023 on).
numbers: Test Brier: system 0.179, crowd 0.149, random 0.250. Accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%. Best raw model without retrieval: GPT-4-1106 at 0.208. Averaging system and crowd gives 0.146, best in every setting. Zou et al. had 65.4% vs a 92.8% crowd on Autocast.
quote: None of the models are naturally good at forecasting.
limits: Same group tuned the system on platform data. Paleka et al. 2025 warn of leakage through retrieval (a22).
agent_relevance: Biggest gains came from retrieval and aggregation, not the base model. Averaging model and crowd beats either. Supports code-side ensembling with an external signal.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) where the system beats or loses to the crowd
finding: System wins when the crowd is unsure, early in a question's life, and when it retrieves many articles. It loses when the crowd is certain, because it rarely outputs extreme probabilities.
numbers: Crowd between 0.3 and 0.7: Brier 0.199 vs crowd 0.246 (validation set). When the crowd is within 0.05 of 0 or 1, the system has 7% higher accuracy but Brier worse by 0.04. System beats crowd on retrieval dates 1-3 but not 4-5.
limits: Rules were found on the validation set and then applied to the test set. Category-level differences are noisy.
agent_relevance: LLMs hedge toward the middle (authors blame safety training). A calibration map that restores extremes, fitted on held-out data, is the analogue of Mandel and Barnes' underconfidence fix.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) calibration and fine-tuning
finding: Zero-shot models are badly calibrated. After fine-tuning and ensembling the system is well calibrated without calibration-specific training.
numbers: Test RMS calibration error: system .42, crowd .38 (as printed in the paper). GPT-4-1106 gives a 0.01-0.03 lower Brier than the other base models they compared.
limits: Calibration figures as printed; not re-computed.
agent_relevance: Ensembling plus filtering to good reasoning traces is a calibration lever. Late-stage questions, where the crowd knows more, are where to defer to an external signal.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: Median of 12 LLMs on 31 binary Metaculus questions matched 925 human forecasters. The LLM median beat the 50% baseline. Pre-registered.
numbers: LLM-crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs 0.25 baseline, t(30) = -2.35, p = 0.026. Human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19); difference t(60) = 0.19, p = 0.850. Equivalence test with d = 0.5 bounds (0.081 Brier) passed (p = 0.017 and 0.040) but was not pre-registered.
limits: Only 31 questions, low power. Bench to the Future authors say it 'likely lacked the statistical power' to detect real gaps. A later version fixed a coding error in the equivalence test.
agent_relevance: Aggregating different models helps, but 31 questions cannot show parity. Do not cite this as proof the crowd is matched.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) per-model results
finding: Individual models differ widely. The best single model (GPT-4) scored near the human crowd; weaker models sat at chance.
numbers: Brier: GPT-4 0.15 (SD 0.11), GPT-4 with Bing 0.16, Bard (PaLM 2) 0.19, Falcon-180B 0.21, Claude 2 0.21, Mistral-7B 0.24, GPT-3.5-Instruct 0.25, Llama-2-70B 0.25, humans 0.19. Model effect F(12,354) = 2.64, p = 0.002; corrected p 0.006.
limits: Small question set. Bing access did not help GPT-4 (0.16 vs 0.15).
agent_relevance: Mixed-model aggregation can approach the strongest member or wash it out. Choose models by tested skill.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) acquiescence bias and human-median exposure
finding: Models lean toward yes: mean forecast was above 50% although outcomes were close to an even split. Showing the human median improved both GPT-4 and Claude 2.
numbers: Mean model prediction 57.35 (SD 20.93), t(1006) = 86.20 vs 50. GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 after seeing the human median (p = 0.003). Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p < 0.001). Size of update tracked the human-model gap, r = 0.88 and 0.87.
limits: Models moved toward the shown median; that is conformity as much as learning.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a shown answer moves the model. Supports G5: a forecaster or judge must not see the majority or a proposed answer, unless that external signal is wanted as an input.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) AI-augmented predictions
finding: Preregistered experiment, N = 991. Humans who could ask an LLM assistant forecast 24-28% more accurately than a control that got a weaker model without numbers, even when the assistant was deliberately noisy and overconfident.
numbers: ANOVA F(2, 988) = 34.58, p < .001. Gain 24%-28% vs control; without one outlier question, 41% for the superforecasting assistant and 29% for the noisy one. Six questions per participant. Power set for Cohen's d = 0.20.
limits: Outlier-driven (one question showed +470% deviation for the noisy arm). The control was a weaker model, so the gain is vs a weak aid, not vs no aid. Tetlock is a co-author.
agent_relevance: A wrong but numeric assistant still helped, so some benefit comes from anchors and structure, not from skill.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Autocast: forecasting future world events with neural networks
finding: First large dataset of tournament questions (Metaculus, INFER, GJOpen) with crowd forecast time series. Retrieval-based models did far worse than the crowd.
numbers: Best model 65% accuracy on true/false vs 92% for the crowd and 50% for random. Crowd forecasts are well calibrated and get more accurate from question start to close.
limits: Pre-2022 models. Crowd baseline is the final aggregate before close, which is easier than earlier forecasts.
agent_relevance: Shows the old gap; the 2023-2024 papers (a12, a15) show it narrowing. A lower anchor for our own evaluation.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting
finding: 1,000 auto-generated, regularly refreshed questions (market and dataset sources). Superforecasters (39 recruited) beat the public median and every LLM.
numbers: Overall Brier: superforecasters 0.096, public median 0.121, best LLM on the 200-question subset Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122 (p < 0.001 vs superforecasters). With combination questions added, superforecasters 0.076 vs GPT-4o 0.130; that 0.054 gap is bigger than the 0.026 gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4.
limits: Few superforecaster answers per question (minimum 3, mean about 8). Missing dataset forecasts imputed at 0.5.
agent_relevance: Best published evidence that a skilled-human aggregate still leads LLMs. First target for our agent: the public-median level; stretch target: superforecaster level.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench trend projection
finding: Linear extrapolation says LLMs reach superforecaster level with higher Arena score or more compute, with wide uncertainty.
numbers: Brier vs Chatbot Arena score r = -0.68, p = 0.003; y = 0.506 - 0.000298x, R2 = 0.47; crossing near Arena 1406 (bootstrap 95% CI 1346-1633). Brier vs log training compute r = -0.67, p = 0.046; crossing at about 6.49e26 FLOP (CI 9.69e25 to 8.65e28).
limits: Few models; extrapolation, not measurement. The compute fit is only marginally significant.
agent_relevance: Do not plan around a date. Capability helps; scaffolds are our lever until then.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating language model forecasters
finding: List of leakage and extrapolation problems that can inflate LLM forecasting claims: logical leakage in backtests, retrieval-date leakage, training-data leakage, label noise, benchmark gaming.
numbers: Worked example: 50 questions at 50% base rate plus 50 at 5%. A forecaster perfect on the rare events scores Brier about 0.125. One who only improves the coin-flips from 0.25 to 0.15 scores about 0.10 and looks better. A base-rate forecaster scores b(1-b).
quote: Accuracy is not a strictly proper scoring rule.
limits: Position paper with examples; does not re-run the cited systems. Flags selecting questions that resolved in a window as a possible logical leak in prior work.
agent_relevance: Score our agent with proper scores, per base-rate bucket, and use pastcasting only with a frozen corpus.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency checks for language model forecasters
finding: Instant, outcome-free metric based on arbitrage over logically related predictions. It correlates with later Brier score, so coherence can proxy skill before outcomes arrive.
numbers: Some consistency metrics reach R > 0.9 correlation with forecasting performance; other logical tests give little signal. Also releases a consistency benchmark that resolves in 2028.
limits: Correlation across a modest number of forecasters; not all checks work.
agent_relevance: Coherence (exclusive answers sum to 1, negation consistency) is a cheap code check, in line with G5 and with coherence recalibration in humans (a07).

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based RL to predict the future
finding: RL on resolved prediction-market questions with a Brier reward trained a 14B model to match o1 on a 1,265-question hold-out and calibrate better.
numbers: Seven-run ReMax ensemble Brier 0.190 [0.178, 0.203], ECE 0.062. o1 Brier 0.202, ECE 0.093. DeepSeek-R1 14B base 0.215, ECE 0.089. The market price still beat the model by 0.039 Brier. Simulated Polymarket profit $52 vs $39 for o1. Plain GRPO tended to collapse toward overconfidence.
limits: Still worse than the market price. Trading simulation ignores costs and market impact. Training, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Median sampling at inference helped. Training was needed for calibration. The market remains the strong signal to combine with.

source: Hambly et al. (2025) Bench to the Future (pastcasting)
finding: Benchmark with frozen offline web corpora for questions whose answers are known, so agents can be tested repeatably. Includes Claude 4 models.
numbers: Mean Brier: Claude Sonnet 3.5 0.1925; 3.5 v2 0.1690; 3.7 0.1712; 3.7 thinking 0.1645; Sonnet 4 0.1560; Sonnet 4 thinking 0.1597; Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.1611. No-evidence forecaster markedly worse. Many pairwise gaps not significant (Sonnet 4 vs 4 thinking p = 0.53).
limits: No human baseline, so absolute Brier cannot be interpreted. Authors say live checks are still needed.
agent_relevance: A leakage-controlled testbed we could use. Thinking mode did not clearly help forecasting; evidence did. Extra reasoning is not the lever.

source: Cross-reading note: human field scores vs LLM scores
finding: Human field Brier (0.074) and LLM Brier (0.15-0.21) are on different questions, horizons and base rates, so they cannot sit on one scale.
numbers: Mandel and Barnes: 96% of forecasts under one year, Brier 0.074. ForecastBench superforecasters 0.096 and Halawi crowd 0.149 are on prediction-site questions chosen to be uncertain.
limits: My synthesis of a02, a06, a12 and a20; no new data.
agent_relevance: Evaluate our agent per difficulty bucket and report skill against a base-rate forecast, not raw Brier.

source: Tetlock (2005) Expert Political Judgment (background, not opened)
finding: Founding long-run study of expert forecasts, the baseline Mandel and Barnes compare against. Only the second-hand numbers in a05 were seen.
numbers: Second-hand via Mandel and Barnes: best forecasters explained about 20% of outcome variance; experts overconfident; experience had no effect.
limits: Not opened. Treat details as unverified until read.
agent_relevance: Needed for the 'experts are overconfident' side of the story that Mandel and Barnes reverse.

source: Baron, Mellers, Tetlock et al. (2014) Two reasons to make aggregated probability forecasts more extreme (background, not opened)
finding: ACE-tournament paper cited by Satopaa and Ungar and by Mandel and Tetlock for extremizing aggregates. Not opened; title and role known only from citations.
numbers: No numbers verified this session.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Read before setting any aggregation rule. Likely the key human evidence for G4 and against extremizing correlated LLM votes.
